text:
Backyard Townhouses / Behin Ha

In Jersey City's Heights district, Backyard Townhouses by Behin Ha transforms a stalled demolition into an opportunity for urban densification. Designed by the studio led by Behrang Behin and Ann Ha, the project restores a nearly 150-year-old house while introducing three contemporary townhouses in its rear yard, nearly tripling the site's residential capacity without altering the historic streetscape.

title: Framing Natural Light: Five Daylighting Strategies in Cabin Architecture
text:
Framing Natural Light: Five Daylighting Strategies in Cabin Architecture

Cabins offer architects opportunities to experiment playfully with architectural form, materials, landscaping, and spatial configurations. Their compact footprints, relatively simple programs, and close proximity to the natural surroundings allow for unconventional design approaches and the ability to test experiential, architectural ideas. Often constructed as spaces of rest, cabin architecture encourages architects to prioritize the experience of inhabiting a space, exploring how individual design elements contribute to the character and atmosphere of the interior.

title: Ersatzneubau Winkel / Kollektiv.w AG
text:
Ersatzneubau Winkel / Kollektiv.w AG

A House in the Green – Nestled between residential buildings and mature trees stood a small former production hall. Originally, it was to be preserved and extended with a senior-friendly apartment, but structural assessments revealed that this would only be possible with extensive interventions. Due to these challenges and the limited space, a replacement building was planned, with a floor plan based on the former hall.

title: What AI Reveals About Architecture That Was Never Built
text:
What AI Reveals About Architecture That Was Never Built

Some architectural projects only survive as drawings, competition entries, or models in archives. Others were built, but not as first imagined, and the completed building gradually replaced the original proposal in collective memory. Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral is familiar to many, but less well known is his Warrant Design, the spire-topped proposal approved in 1675 that he subsequently reworked as construction progressed. London was also once offered a very different monument: Thomas Willson's vast pyramid-shaped necropolis for Primrose Hill, designed to accommodate millions of burials and dominate the city's skyline.

title: Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 Announces Opening Programme Featuring Performances, Films, and Conference
text:
Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 Announces Opening Programme Featuring Performances, Films, and Conference

The Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has announced the opening programme of its third edition, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures. Curated by writer and anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, with Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the Triennial will take place from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, with its six-day opening programme running from November 14 to 19. Co-curated by Rao and Sharmeen Inayat, SAT's Research and Civic Engagement Curator, the programme brings together participatory projects, live performances, film screenings, lectures, and discussions across the Emirate of Sharjah, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19.

title: Bringing Hospitality-Inspired Textures into Workplace Interiors
text:
Bringing Hospitality-Inspired Textures into Workplace Interiors

"We can really bring a hospitality look into a workplace, which is something that our clients have been asking for, for many years," says Mark Harder, a design director at Gensler. The warmth of wood, the texture of leather, and the tactile surfaces found in hotels and restaurants are also sought in offices, airports, and shared corridors. Bringing these qualities into different settings, however, requires considering how materials will respond to everyday use.

title: A Garden City in the Caribbean: Planning Belize’s New Capital, Belmopan
text:
A Garden City in the Caribbean: Planning Belize’s New Capital, Belmopan

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

title: Khao Phra Tamnak House / SPACE | STORY | STUDIO
text:
Khao Phra Tamnak House / SPACE | STORY | STUDIO

Set on the gentle hillside of Khao Phra Tamnak, the house is conceived through a flexible design diagram rather than a predetermined architectural form. The project begins with the conditions of the place and the lives to be accommodated: a gradual change in land level, the family's need for generous and usable flat spaces, the principles of Feng Shui, and the presence of neighboring homes. These factors are not treated as separate constraints. They are brought together in a framework that can be tested, adjusted, and extended.

title: Homes Around Trees / architectureRED
text:
Homes Around Trees / architectureRED

Urban housing in India stands at the intersection of rapid urbanization and a shifting sense of identity. The pressures of land scarcity and market-driven development have transformed housing into a commodity, often prioritizing maximum yield over the fundamental idea of home. In the process, the very essence of housing—as a space that fosters identity, community, and rootedness — is increasingly eroded. The relentless stacking of units, the erasure of open space, and the homogenization of urban environments leave little room for meaningful engagement with nature or with each other.

text:
Tabasco 267 Apartment / CAAM Arquitectos

Tabasco 267 is the renovation of a 90 m² apartment in the Roma Norte neighborhood of Mexico City. CAAM used the existing conditions as the project's raw material, transforming the layout, ceilings, finishes, lighting, and furniture.

title: Sewing Atelier Studio / Atelier 77 + Matéria Base
text:
Sewing Atelier Studio / Atelier 77 + Matéria Base

Located in the historic neighborhood of Santa Teresa in Rio de Janeiro, this sewing studio occupies a platform surrounded by a stone retaining wall, built over 200 years ago, according to local reports. This pre-existing structure establishes the architectural concept, serving both as a physical boundary and structural support for the new intervention.

title: Coco House / CVA Arquitectos
text:
Coco House / CVA Arquitectos

Living immersed in nature. House and nature are conceived as an indissoluble entity. Designed as a weekend refuge for the architect herself and her dog "Coco," the project synthesizes her personal quest to live immersed in nature. This search began with the idea of carefully integrating the volume with the existing vegetation and connecting it precisely to the natural terrain. In this way, the house harmoniously adapts to the steep slope, merging with it and becoming an integral part of the landscape.

title: House in Beloura / ARX Portugal Arquitectos
text:
House in Beloura / ARX Portugal Arquitectos

The house is positioned on the site with the aim of responding in a relatively simple way to two central questions: How can it capture a panoramic view of the horizon, which also brings us the presence of the sea? How can it embrace outdoor spaces that simultaneously protect the residents' privacy from neighbors' views and ensure comfort on days of strong wind?

title: French Creek Workshops House / Wittman Estes
text:
French Creek Workshops House / Wittman Estes

This home for a newly retired couple sits beside a wetland on a four-and-a-half-acre site once used as an animal sanctuary. Conceived as a serene retreat immersed in nature, it offers comfort and beauty throughout the seasons, sheltering its occupants during the cool, rainy months and opening outward during the dry, warm season.

title: MKR Store in Seville / Guillermo Vázquez Consuegra
text:
MKR Store in Seville / Guillermo Vázquez Consuegra

The refurbishment Project for the multilabel shop MKR arises from the demand of reorganizing and giving a new image to the existing retail space: an unstructured and limited space, not in compliance with the actual regulatory standards.

title: Rustoordlaan / Atelier M Architects + Planners bv
text:
Rustoordlaan / Atelier M Architects + Planners bv

Nestled within Heuvelhofpark in Kessel-Lo (BE) lies the new replacement housing project for the social housing company Dijledal. To maximize the preservation of the existing trees and the park, the building's footprint was kept highly compact and rotated 17 degrees. Wrapped in light green terracotta panels and finished with reseda green windows, the 30 units offer residents the ultimate luxury: a living experience right up among the treetops.

title: Human-Centered Design: How does design shape the way we live, feel, and connect?
text:
Human-Centered Design: How does design shape the way we live, feel, and connect?

To say that we design "for people" seems like a fundamental premise of architecture. However, this statement presents a problem: people are not a homogeneous category.

Human-Centered Design invites us to question whom we observe, listen to, and represent when making design decisions. Through an interdisciplinary conversation, we will explore how physical, sensory, and social needs influence architecture and interior design, and how these shape our way of living, feeling, and connecting.

Drawing from the fields of health, air transport, education, urban planning, and architectural representation, various perspectives will bring these priorities into dialogue.

title: Design by numbers: is AI ruining UX or just pouring gasoline on the fire?
text:
Design by numbers: is AI ruining UX or just pouring gasoline on the fire?

Everyone seems to be asking whether AI will replace UX designers. I think that’s the wrong question.

In March 2025, the Computer History Museum and IEEE Spectrum staged a debate on a single question: when a large language model answers you, does it even understand what it’s saying? Does it comprehend what the words mean, or is it only predicting which word comes next?

Emily Bender, a linguist at the University of Washington, argued it’s only predicting. In fact, she has a name for these systems: stochastic parrots, machines that string words together by probability, the way a parrot repeats sounds, with no idea what any of it really means. Sébastien Bubeck, a researcher at OpenAI, took the opposite stance. Understanding, he argued, is in the eye of the beholder, and you judge it by what a system does.

“Let’s say I want to build an app, and I ask one of those models to build the app for me… I just specify in natural language what I want, I come back the next day and, boom, the app is there. Did the model understand on the way of creating this? In a way, I don’t really care. It did something for me.”

Let’s unpack this statement, because I think it’s a fairly common argument and also one that is dangerously misleading. Not only does this misrepresent how designers actually work, but the real danger is in the shrug. It lacks accountability. Once you stop caring whether AI understands what it’s doing, then you shift your measure of success away from outcomes and toward output.

UX design exists to make things work for the people who use them. Can the user complete a task easily and intuitively? That’s the outcome. The things designers produce along the way (journey maps, wireframes, prototypes, etc.) are outputs. They’re evidence of a process; they aren’t proof that anyone’s life got easier.

AI is a bit like a microwave — it will cook your food faster but not as well. Successful products are not ones that get made as quickly as possible but ones that resonate with users. A TV dinner is not fine dining. When we remove empathy and understanding from the deliverable, we risk delivering bad experiences that may not actually solve user pain points. Ignoring that is a treacherous path.

For the past year, I’ve spent eight or more hours a day designing with a range of AI tools. I’ve built everything from Chrome extensions to websites to enterprise-level multi-agent orchestration workflows. What I’ve learned is that, even for an experienced UX designer, this is no small feat. It requires tireless attention to detail over weeks or months to get a usable product from AI. It does not happen overnight, and it takes a hell of a lot of natural language cursing to get there.

What Bubeck is describing is a proof of concept, and a proof of concept is very different from a well-designed product. It shows that something can exist; it doesn’t show that it works for the people who will use it. By Bubeck’s own assertion that we should judge a system by what it does, the overnight app doesn’t pass muster.

Once that first, overnight build is in, what follows is actual UX design: noticing that the flow is wrong, that an error state is missing, that users get hung up in closed-loop modals. When we rush the first iteration, it can take a great deal of time and effort on the back end to repair these issues, especially if we’re trying to explain them to a tool that doesn’t understand what it’s doing.

But, if we’re being honest, this is not a problem that started with AI. Bubeck’s assertion comes from a misunderstanding of design that’s decades old: that the job is about outputs, rather than outcomes. So is AI really what we should be worried about here, or is it just pouring gasoline on a fire that was already burning?

But first: Is AI taking UX jobs?

Every few weeks, someone asks me whether I’m worried about losing my job to AI. All the headlines, the LinkedIn posts, and the steady stream of clickbait declaring that “designers are finished” make this an obvious question to ask, and I think I’m in a decent position to address it. As a design lead, I use AI tools every day — everything from Codex to Claude, IDEs, Mistral, Copilots, n8n, and GitHub Actions. I even developed my own VS Code extension to orchestrate cross-model prompt chaining. When I get spare time, I lecture about the history and impact of human-computer interaction at the university level.

I won’t pretend nothing has changed. Layoffs are real, and I’ve seen them firsthand, but the numbers are anecdotal. The only hard counts are tech-wide, not design-specific.

The best public data I could find for open design jobs comes from two sources: Indeed’s postings index for design and UX, and the job tracker TrueUp, which covers tech companies and startups. Indeed shows postings more than doubling from early 2021 to a peak in early 2022, then dropping roughly 70% by mid-2023. Most of this happened before anyone had ever heard of ChatGPT. TrueUp shows the same drop and what came after. Since autumn of 2023, it has kept mostly stable around 2,200, with a brief spike in spring 2026 before settling back down again.

That’s what a correction after a hiring surge looks like, and it doesn’t necessarily correlate with the spread of AI. If AI were driving these numbers, I’d expect the line to keep falling as the tools spread. Yet, Figma’s 2026 State of the Designer report found that 72% of the designers it surveyed are using generative AI. That doesn’t disprove AI is playing a role in the job market; it just means the data doesn’t show AI as a negative catalyst.

But still we feel the squeeze, and part of it may simply be supply and demand: too many new designers chasing the same amount of openings. Nobody publishes how many people are newly entering the UX field, or how many unemployed designers there are at each level, but a quick LinkedIn search for “UX designer” showed that the first 25 postings had already passed LinkedIn’s display cap of “Over 100” applicants. That’s just one search (and these applicants aren’t necessarily all out of work) but it does give you an idea of what looking for a job right now is like.

Put together, these numbers don’t really describe a sea change of job loss. AI doesn’t seem to be changing whether the jobs exist so much as what the jobs are. I’m less afraid of losing my job to AI than I am of the job itself becoming unrecognizable. Design has been misunderstood for decades, and if we’re not careful, AI agents will let that misunderstanding become the job description, leaving the user experience to chance.

Design (without) thinking

I believe true UX designers are a rare breed. The work is a combination of critical thinking, empathy, and taste. These are things you can’t really teach, and they’re also things that AI fundamentally lacks.

I say that as someone who teaches and has seen the limits of what teaching can accomplish. A course can show you how to run a usability test or build a journey map, but it can’t make you care whether the person on the other side struggled. It can’t give you the instinct that something is off before you can say exactly what. What a course can teach is process, and that’s where AI and human designers both get tripped up: it’s hard to empathize when you’re following a prescribed process. Thoughtlessly following processes can imitate outputs, but not outcomes.

The trouble is that process is visible and ability is not, so the two are often conflated. You can see a workshop, journey maps, or wireframes, but you can’t see the judgment that decided what question to ask during a user interview, or when to challenge the obvious solution. When design is reduced to a checklist of methods and deliverables, it’s easier to report what has been delivered, but a team can run a flawless process and still deliver an unusable product.

This is what I mean by “design by numbers”: the fallacy that if you follow the steps and produce the artifacts, good design is guaranteed at the end.

But where did this misunderstanding come from? In the 1960s, the design methods movement set out to “scientise” design into a linear process that anyone could follow and repeat. Some of its own pioneers later turned against this idea, describing the attempt to make design scientific as a misguided effort to turn dynamic problem solving into a linear, repeatable process. They argued that the problems designers face don’t sit still long enough to be universal. Horst Rittel called these “wicked” problems: ill-formulated, with confusing information, many decision makers with conflicting values, and consequences that ripple through the whole system.

Design is not a linear, repeatable process, and it never was. There is no single path to a solution waiting to be found.

I liken it to IKEA assembly instructions: you can follow the steps and build a perfectly fine shelf, but what if now you need to build a table or paint a wall? Would you use the same instructions? Or even the same tools?

Design thinking, the most widely used methodology in the field, is a genuinely good way to get a team collaborating. In practice, though, it can devolve into a clutter of sticky notes that no one will ever look at again, with designers speculating about what stakeholders actually need, think, and feel. Graphic designer Natasha Jen made this point in her talk Design Thinking Is Bullsh*t. She regretted that design practice had been reduced to a defined sequence of steps, and argued that “real designers surround themselves with evidence.” When we limit ourselves to preconceived processes, we may be the ones preventing ourselves from solving what looks impossible. Writer and designer John Thackara offers a better frame, which he calls sense-and-respond design, where you describe the desired outcomes but not the detailed means of reaching them.

That can be a bitter pill to swallow for stakeholders who need to report quarterly deliverables, but here’s the thing: users don’t care about deliverables — they care whether a product works for them. And that outcome depends on whether designers have the time and ability to understand what they are doing.

Slop is as slop does

If you believe process and output is the job of design, then AI might look like a handy replacement. It produces outputs quickly and confidently: personas, flows, copy — even working prototypes. And designers aren’t resisting that. In the Figma survey, 89% of designers using generative AI said it makes them faster, and I’d say the same about my own work. AI is a genuinely useful tool, but it’s a tool like any other. Generating these artifacts is only part of a designer’s job, and it’s the part that doesn’t require critical thinking, empathy, or taste.

When I talk to my students about how to work with AI, I like to separate tasks into two different categories: thinking and doing.

AI is good at doing. In my experience, that typically includes three things in UX design:

  • Synthesizing user research. It can take a pile of interview notes or survey responses and group, summarize and surface patterns far faster than I can by hand. That’s the legwork. What the patterns mean for the product is still mine to decide.
  • Meta-work. Slide decks, readouts, summaries and the other work about the work. It’s necessary and it takes time, but none of it is the design itself.
  • Translating mockups into prototypes. Once I’ve decided what the experience should be, AI can turn the mockups into something clickable much faster than I could build it myself. But the design work I do at the whiteboard is still the source of truth.

Designers can let AI do things for them. But it should never think for them. There’s a name for this: automation bias, the tendency to trust what an automated system hands us over our own judgment. A hammer is an incredibly useful tool, but would you let a hammer think for you? Deciding what the problem is, what the research means, what to build, and what’s good enough requires critical thinking skills, and that’s where AI stops and the designer’s judgment takes over. When we outsource our thinking to AI, what comes back might look like a solid answer but is really just stochastic parroting from something that doesn’t understand the problem.

AI is a translation tool. It can turn natural language into code very quickly, but it doesn’t understand how to ask the right questions. It can’t properly architect a product, and it frequently misses visual bugs that are glaringly obvious to a real designer.

When anyone can generate a prototype in an afternoon, a prototype stops being evidence of anything important. In a world where AI slop is cheap and fast, the designer’s ability to discern good design from bad and to ask whether we’re solving the right problem becomes more important, not less.

When the enshittification hits the fan

The more I work with AI, the more I see a need to change the way we think about design.

The pressure starts with expectations. If the story is that you can “come back the next day and, boom, the app is there,” then someone down the hall will ask why designing the first MVP has taken two weeks. A proof of concept gets mistaken for the product, timelines compress, and the output gets treated as the outcome.

Figma’s survey lists unrealistic timelines among the things that stand in the way of designers doing their best work. AI puts that into a pressure cooker because the artifacts can be built faster than we can understand them. With an expedited delivery timeline, the first things to go are the parts that are hard to report: talking to the people who will use the product, testing, critiquing, discovering you are wrong and then iterating as you learn. These things look like delays when AI can just cut straight to the end result.

But there’s a problem with jumping straight to the end: it’s reckless. Letting AI build products for you creates a kind of house of mirrors that only the AI knows how to navigate. Because of context limits, it builds piecemeal, one function at a time, supplanting holistic architecture for a labyrinth of myopic patches. The result is a product that might work but that nobody really understands. I can’t tell you the number of times I’ve had to prompt AI to refactor an entire codebase because it lacked any architectural spine. Say goodbye to your tokens.

Building products this way also shifts the means of production out of your business and into the hands of a few AI companies (OpenAI and Anthropic, to name a few). Your business ends up relying on agent subscriptions and usage limits to stay in operation, while your own employees become less skilled. That should be a very dubious prospect for any business owner.

We’re already starting to see what this shift looks like day to day. A product manager I worked with recently surprised me one day with designs he’d made using AI. He was visibly excited about what he’d created, but to me they were a jumbled mess: no hierarchy, no clear calls to action, useless icons on every surface… To someone who isn’t a designer, they probably looked fine. That’s the trick with these tools. They sound like they know what they’re talking about, but only to people who don’t know what they’re talking about.

And this is not just a design problem. It’s becoming more and more pervasive across disciplines. Designers using AI can see the flaws in its designs just like developers can see the flaws in its code. So the next time you vibe-code something, understand that what you’re creating is not a finished product that any god-fearing developer would bless.

The key here is to maintain accountability by learning to spot the warning signs. Is a PM asking AI instead of doing market research? Red flag. Is a designer using AI as a beta tester instead of talking to actual users? Red flag. Did a stakeholder say everything looks good on a call, then immediately dump five paragraphs of feedback into Slack? Maybe start to question how much thought actually went into that.

We need to get into the habit of not limiting our focus to artifacts and output and instead ask deeper questions about how we are creating better experiences. If you can answer that, you’ll be fine with or without AI. And if you can’t — or don’t really care — you’re going to have bigger problems than any tool can fix.

AI is a powerful tool, and in the hands of someone who understands its limitations, it can make the work easier. The open question is who gets to decide how it’s used, and whether they understand the difference between producing an output and enabling an outcome.

What businesses need to understand is that design is qualitative, not quantitative. It can’t be reduced to steps and artifacts, and it can’t be measured by how much gets produced. Design is a conversation between the business and its users that says “we’ve thought about this more than you’ll ever have to.” The companies that stand apart will be the ones that invest in that level of thinking. The companies that outsource their thinking to AI will get the same slop as everyone else.

title: Everyone’s got a quick question
text:
Everyone’s got a quick question

And you shouldn’t have to answer them all.

There’s an interactive version of this story. Explore it →

I became the team’s search engine

Every team has a person everyone reaches out to. They know where things live, why a decision went the way it did, and who to ask when you’re stuck. If you’re on a team, you’ve probably messaged yours today. 😏

In Radical Candor, Kim Scott calls the steady, dependable people a team is built on its rock stars. Our team has a few too many sports fans, so we call ours the GOAT: the greatest of all time.

I lead a remote design team of fifteen, and a lot of the team’s questions find their way to me. Each seems small enough on its own, but the constant interruptions were starting to wear on me. 🫣

And apparently, there’s research behind that frustration: a 2008 CHI paper found that people often work faster to make up for interruptions, but feel more stressed and frustrated as a result.

I wondered how many of these interruptions were actually necessary. So I reviewed two and a half years of requests — 2,413 in total — and sorted them by what it took to answer. That led Bryan, my intern, and me to build a Slack agent to take some of them off my plate.

What was in my inbox

At my busiest, about nine housekeeping requests reached me every workday, close to fifty a week. Spread across a calendar, they filled almost every workday.

Some questions kept coming back

Plenty felt like déjà vu. 203 had been asked before, some more than a dozen times. The most repeated — how to access user study recordings — came up 32 times. My guess is that most repeats happened in DMs, where nobody else could see the answer. And even in public channels, how often does anyone dig through old Slack threads?

The wait by hour

Most of my designers are part-timers who work their own hours, often in the evening, while I keep a nine to five. During the day, I tried to get back to people as soon as I could, usually within about 15 minutes (allow me to feel proud of myself for a second 😎). Outside working hours, however, a question could wait 12 to 13 hours, until I was back the next morning.

Did these all need me?

Not really. After going through the cases carefully, I found that 53% didn’t need me at all. The answer already existed somewhere, in a doc, a Figma file or an old thread; people just couldn’t find it, or didn’t know it was there. Another 35% were mostly legwork, like digging up which spec was current or what a handoff thread had settled, before I signed off. The last 12% were the calls only I could make: someone’s role, their hours, who should help with what.

Most questions didn’t need my judgment. They just needed an answer

Could an agent answer them?

I’ll admit, I’d been quietly “cheating” on the easy questions: paste them into my own agent, check the answer, and pass it along in my own words. It worked often enough that I wondered, why not let the team ask directly? So Bryan and I built a quick Slack prototype. We called it le goat 🐐 (my fellow LeBron fans, iykyk).

Here’s what happened when I tried an easy one. A small server on Cloudflare picked up the mention and reacted with 👀, so whoever asked knew le goat was on it. It kept track of the thread and handed the question to Gemini, which looked things up in Notion, GitHub and the web, then wrote back in the same thread.

It worked, but a simple question could get a 639-word essay in return. I’d feel really guilty dropping that on someone in Slack. le goat needed work.

Making it a bot with manners

Before anyone else saw it, I taught it how to reply. Much of the interaction design was inspired by principles in Google’s People + AI Guidebook, especially around communicating uncertainty, handling errors, and keeping people in control. The challenge was making those principles feel natural in a Slack conversation.

  • Show it’s working. A question used to meet four silent minutes, then the bot’s inner monologue. Now “Thinking” appears right away, with the steps folded under it and a Stop button.
  • Get to the point. The answer used to hide in paragraph two. Now it comes first, in one line. A comparison becomes a small table, and counts become bars.
  • Know what you don’t know. One of our developers loves quoting Socrates: real wisdom is knowing what you don’t know. Instead of a confident claim with nothing behind it, le goat now says what it couldn’t find and who would know, and its sources fold away under one tap.
  • Leave the calls to people. Instead of editing our guidelines without asking, le goat drafts the change, like an update to a doc or a new card, and never makes it itself. The draft arrives on a card in Slack, and nothing changes until the right person approves it.

The MVP for everyday questions

With its manners in place, I scoped the MVP to the five kinds of questions people asked me most often: finding something (314 asks), catching up on what they missed (565), knowing who to ask (448), asking for design-system guidance (731), and turning a discussion into a card.

A tryout with the team

For the pilot, I invited the whole team to try le goat and ask it anything in Slack. And they kept asking: 228 questions in two weeks, averaging 31 a day in week two. That’s more than three times my busiest week.

They wanted it in the flow

The funny thing about giving people an agent they can ask anything: they start wanting it everywhere. Designers wanted le goat in Figma, where they spend their day, so we built that. Now they can @le goat in a Figma comment and get a reply right there.

From answering to asking

People were clearly using le goat. But I also wanted to know if I could trust its answers.

Competent, but not confident

So I checked 56 of its answers for hallucinations. Luckily, none were confidently wrong. But only 37 were confident and right. The other 19, about one in three, came back unsure. That’s a lot of uncertainty for an agent meant to unblock the team.

What puzzled me was that the answers seemed well grounded. The tools were connected, and the sources were cited correctly. So why was le goat so unsure?

Here’s one of those 19 cases, recreated. Someone asked how big the field labels on our forms should be. le goat found three answers: the Forms PRD in Notion said TBD, Figma said 13px, and the code said 14px. It couldn’t tell which was current.

Finding the answers wasn’t the problem. Knowing which one to trust was.

Why the docs disagreed

To see how they drifted apart, I lined up the sources chronologically. A PM asked about the field-label size, and the PRD recorded TBD. Design later settled on 13px, and the code followed. But the PRD never caught up, and an unrelated refactor eventually changed the code to 14px. No wonder le goat was unsure.

This is partly a team coordination problem. Practices like Atlassian’s working agreements help clarify how teams work together and where decisions live. But decisions change, and documentation doesn’t always keep up.

A proactive teammate

And this wasn’t the only time our sources disagreed. Of the 2,413 asks, 204 (8.5%) were people checking which version of something was right. Those were some of the best questions I got. They helped catch discrepancies and kept the team aligned.

A real GOAT doesn’t just answer questions. They know which questions need asking.

So I wondered if le goat could do that too. That became the idea behind the next iteration: making it a proactive teammate that could speak up on its own, in three ways.

Shares the FYI. Decisions don’t always reach everyone who needs to know. So le goat sends a short morning update every day with what’s changed and where it was decided.

Flags the discrepancy. Every Monday, le goat checks for sources that don’t agree. Instead of just raising questions, it brings the right people the evidence and a proposed fix to review.

Follows through. Fixes can slip through the cracks. When one goes unreviewed, le goat checks whether it’s already been handled before sending the owner a reminder.

Every accepted fix leaves a cleaner source. And with each owner only reviewing their part, nobody has to maintain everything alone. A little divide & conquer.

A few tweaks under the hood

For anyone curious about the tech, here are a few nerdy improvements I made since the first prototype.

Classification. Not every message needs the same amount of thinking (or spending 🤑). Jev, a small, fast model, classifies messages first: simple ones get a prescribed reply, while real questions go to the LLM with an appropriate thinking level.

Connector expansion. We added Figma and our service knowledge base through Supabase, alongside Notion, GitHub and the web. That’s how we got le goat answering directly in Figma comments: a webhook picks up the mention, and the reply goes back into the same thread.

Permissions. We made le goat aware of where it’s speaking — public channels, private channels or DMs — to avoid oversharing sensitive information. People can opt in by linking their Slack account, letting le goat search their private conversations while keeping the answers visible only to them.

Triple-double for the team

I tracked three things to see if le goat helped: how many questions still reached me, how long people waited, and how often it was confident and right. All three improved. And the answers now live in shared threads, where the next person can find them.

Setting the GOAT free

Every team needs someone who knows where things live, why decisions were made, and who owns what. But their days shouldn’t go to answering the same questions.

le goat takes care of the everyday asks, freeing those people for the work that needs them: hard design calls, riffing on ideas, pushing boundaries, and raising the ceiling.

There’s a bigger benefit, too. As agents become part of everyday work, a reliable knowledge base matters even more. Fewer discrepancies mean fewer made-up answers and better information for people and agents alike.

Let le goat handle the busywork, so the real GOATs have time for the hard work.

What’s next: the agent farm

Now that le goat is out of the barn, I’ve been thinking about recruiting a few teammates. A sassy owl for critiques, a diligent mule for the dirty work, a quick horse for urgent requests. Every GOAT needs a team, right?

Further reading

A few resources that informed this work or offer useful perspectives on the challenges discussed:

  • Radical Candor — Kim Scott. On building effective teams and recognizing the contributions of rock stars and superstars.
  • The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress — Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith & Ulrich Klocke (CHI 2008). On the hidden costs of workplace interruptions.
  • People + AI Guidebook — Google PAIR. On designing AI interactions around uncertainty, trust, and human control.
  • Working Agreements — Atlassian Team Playbook. On establishing shared expectations for how teams communicate and make decisions.

title: In a world of panic, calm and certainty win
text:
In a world of panic, calm and certainty win

While panic around what AI means for our industry is the reflex right now, calm is a decision. The calm that comes from knowing what you actually know is the rarest and most valuable thing you can bring to a moment like this.

I recently turned 50 and reckoning with that did what it does to so many people. It made me think. Not in a hauntingly dramatic, staring-out-the-window way, but in an introspective way where you start taking stock of what you’ve actually learned, what still rattles you, and what has stopped rattling you entirely.

That thinking rooted itself from a conversation I had with Skift founder Rafat Ali. When he found out my birthday was coming, he got genuinely excited for me, which is not how most people react to 50. He told me the day after my birthday would be the best day of my life, because that’s when you get to put the whole thing behind you. He said that you just stop carrying the pressure you put on yourself and the pressure you imagine everyone else is putting on you.

That conversation quickly moved on from my age and on to work, to his industry and to what AI is doing to all of it. Without noticing, Rafat said the same thing again in a completely different context.

“There’s so much uncertainty,” he told me, “that the people who stay calm and certain are the ones everyone listens to. In a moment where nobody knows what’s happening, calm is the whole advantage.”

I haven’t stopped thinking about that since.

Those two pieces of advice are actually one piece of advice. The relief Rafat promised me about 50, the freedom of putting down the need to prove yourself, is the exact thing that makes a person valuable in a moment like this one.

The whole industry is panicking about AI. The people who come out of it fine will be the ones who already learned how to put the panic down.

The fear is real

The numbers are striking.

Pew Research found that 71 percent of Americans now think AI will mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, up from 64 percent two years earlier, and among adults under 30 it’s 73 percent. Pew is careful to note that number reflects what people expect, not jobs that have actually been lost.

ADP’s global study of more than thirty-nine thousand people, led by their chief economist Nela Richardson, found that anxiety, not confidence, is now the defining feeling workers have about their work.

A survey from the Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center found nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest polled.

It has gotten real enough that it’s showing up in doctors’ offices. Dr. Simbiat Adighije described a patient who couldn’t stop checking the news, couldn’t stop imagining which parts of her job and her identity might be automated next, and made a point worth holding onto

The anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it ever comes true, the same way climate anxiety is legitimate no matter what you think of any particular model.

This isn’t in your head. The ground is actually moving, and anyone who says otherwise is lying to your face.

Look closely at that Pew number, though, because it’s quite telling. The dread is at an all-time high, and it’s a forecast, a thing people expect, running well ahead of what has actually happened to them. That gap, between how frightened people are and what has actually changed in their own working lives, is where panic lives.

Fear and panic are not the same thing. Fear is a reasonable response to a real risk. Panic is what happens when the fear starts making your decisions for you.

The clinical psychologist Zachary Sikora says that fear is literally our survival response, useful, hardwired, and designed to keep us alive. When it spikes, however, it impairs the part of the brain that handles reasoning and judgment, the exact faculties you need most when things are uncertain.

The more afraid you get, the worse you think.

We have seen this exact panic before

Every big technological shift runs the same arc.

Dora Czerna traced it across decades of disruptions and named the stages. First comes democratization, when a tool suddenly lets a lot more people do something that used to take an expert. Then comes panic, when the experts realize it. Then a stretch of genuine quality collapse, when all those new people flood the zone with mediocre work. Eventually, new norms settle in, and the field is bigger and different and mostly fine.

When desktop publishing arrived, it gave us a decade of ransom-note flyers with twelve fonts on them, and then it gave us a generation of designers who could do more than any typesetter ever could.

The panic comes for everyone. Whether you give in to it is up to you.

This isn’t simply a modern problem. Calestous Juma, who spent years studying how societies react to new technology, found the same pattern running back six hundred years. Coffee, refrigeration, mechanized farming, electricity, every one of them met a wave of fear and resistance before it became ordinary.

The fear, he found, was rarely really about the technology, but rather about people sensing they might lose a piece of their identity or their livelihood, feeling it first and reaching for the evidence afterward.

Economist Derek Thompson has pointed out that the single strongest argument for AI not causing some overnight jobs apocalypse is one word, history. New technology has been reshaping work for centuries, and the story is always the same. The technology shows up, the work changes, and it almost always goes slower and messier than anyone predicted in the panic.

I’ve certainly experienced my own smaller versions of this. The web was going to make everyone a designer, and then it didn’t. The bootcamps were going to flood the field and end the profession, and then they didn’t.

Every time this happens, the panic feels like the end of something, and every time it turns out to be the loud, ugly middle of something, the part right before the new normal shows up and everyone forgets they were ever that scared.

Panic in a downturn is the go-to emotion, even at the top. Nancy Koehn, who studies how leaders handle crises, points to research showing that more than half of leaders become more closed-minded and controlling when a crisis hits, and more than four in ten get angrier and more reactive. The steadiness we remember in the leaders who got it right, the Lincolns and the Shackletons, was always the rare response, which is exactly why it resonates so well.

None of this means the fear is wrong. It means the fear is a stage, and stages pass, especially for the people who don’t let it take over.

The calm that wins is the kind you earn

There’s a version of calm that’s just denial, the person insisting nothing is changing while the ground shifts under them. Plugging your ears with your fingers, screaming “la la la la la,” hoping the phase just passes you by.

That’s not what Rafat was describing in our conversation. The calm that actually wins is the kind you earn, the kind that comes from knowing what you’re good at, having done the work enough times to trust your own informed point-of-view, and no longer needing to prove any of it to anyone.

ADP’s global study found that the workers using AI the most heavily reported significantly less stress than the ones barely touching it, about half as many said they felt overloaded.

Ethan Mollick has been saying for years that the people who get their hands on AI, who learn its edges and its failures firsthand, are the ones who stop fearing it and start using it well.

Familiarity is what turns a vague threat into a known quantity. The dread lives in the gap between you and the thing you’re afraid of.

Patrick Neeman argues that the way out of AI anxiety is to trade the vague fear, the sense that you’re falling behind because everyone else seems to get it, for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work. Vague is the natural state of panic. Specific is the natural state of calm.

The discomfort of being visibly bad at something new, Neeman writes, is just the cost of staying in the game.

This is where Rafat Ali’s point-of-view comes back in, because it turns out his advice wasn’t a passing mood. Ali actually built his whole company around it. When he relaunched Skift in September 2026, he wrote that AI is making information cheaper every month and judgment more valuable, and the three things that never get cheaper are knowledge nobody else has, a point of view on what it means, and access to the people who make the decisions.

The calm he promised me and the strategy he bet his company on are the same thing. Both come from being secure in the one thing the machine can’t hand you.

In a moment when no one is sure what’s happening, the calm, informed person doesn’t just steady themselves, they become the one everyone else steadies against. That is the oldest definition of leadership there is.

The reason panic is such a bad trade is that it spends all your energy on the part you can’t control, the speed of the technology, and none on the part you can, the judgment you bring to it.

The future is a design problem

There’s a specific cost to the panic that most people miss.

Gallup found that when a worker crosses over into believing their job is likely to be eliminated, their engagement drops, their burnout climbs, their satisfaction falls, and they become measurably more likely to start looking for the exit. The belief does the damage, often well before the technology does anything at all.

Panic is not a neutral way to wait out a storm. It quietly degrades the exact things, your focus, your judgment, your work, that you’d need to come through it well.

The real question is what you do with the uncertainty instead. Economist David Autor argues that the AI future should not be not treated as a prediction exercise, but rather as a design problem,.

We tend to talk about what’s coming as though it’s weather, something to forecast and brace for. Autor’s point is that we have enormous say in how it actually goes, through the choices we make and the things we decide to build.

The future isn’t something you wait to find out. It’s something you have a hand in making.

Economists aren’t the only ones saying this. Carolyn Dewar, who advises chief executives at McKinsey, bluntly says that AI won’t decide the future, the people leading through it will.

That’s really a description of what leadership has always been. The best leaders stay calm when no one else does. They get informed instead of getting loud, and they keep making clear-eyed decisions while everyone around them spins out.

A moment of maximum uncertainty is exactly when that kind of person becomes most valuable.

Panic is abdication. Calm, informed, and decisive drives success.

That is the difference between panic and calm. One treats the future as weather, something you brace for and can’t change. The other treats it as a problem, which is a thing you already know how to handle.

Which brings me back to Rafat Ali and to the thing he told me about turning 50. The relief he promised was finally putting away the weight of trying to prove you belong, and discovering that what’s left underneath is everything you actually know how to do. That’s the same calm that wins right now, the calm of someone who has stopped bracing for the future and started building their small corner of it.

You can spend this moment frightened of what AI might take from you or you can get quiet, take stock of what you actually bring, and go to work.The people who come through this just fine are already doing the second thing. They put the panic down, and they got back to the part that was always theirs.

References and further reading

The fear is real

  • Pew Research Center, Americans Are Increasingly Wary of AI. The survey finding that 71 percent of Americans expect AI to mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, rising to 73 percent among adults under 30.
  • Nela Richardson and ADP Research, Today at Work. A global study of more than thirty-nine thousand workers finding that anxiety, not confidence, now defines how people feel about their jobs.
  • Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center, The AI Anxiety Era. A survey finding nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest.
  • Dr. Simbiat Adighije, Anticipatory Anxiety About AI Is Showing Up in Clinic (KevinMD). A psychiatrist on treating patients for AI dread, and why the anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it comes true.
  • Zachary Sikora, 5 Things You Never Knew About Fear (Northwestern Medicine). On fear as a survival response, and how it impairs the brain’s reasoning and judgment when it spikes.

We have seen this panic before

  • Dora Czerna, Disruption Has a Shape. A designer tracing the recurring arc of technological disruption, democratization, panic, quality collapse, then new norms.
  • Calestous Juma, Why Do People Resist New Technologies? (World Economic Forum). A Harvard professor on six hundred years of fear and resistance to new technology, from coffee to electricity.
  • Derek Thompson, Why America’s AI Discourse Feels So Broken. On history as the strongest argument that AI won’t cause an overnight jobs apocalypse.
  • Nancy Koehn, Leadership Under Pressure (Harvard Business School). On research showing most leaders turn closed-minded and reactive in a crisis, and why the steady ones are rare.

The calm that wins is earned

  • Ethan Mollick, Doing Stuff with AI (One Useful Thing). On why the people who get their hands on AI, and learn its edges firsthand, stop fearing it and start using it well.
  • Patrick Neeman, AI Wants Builders. On trading the vague fear of falling behind for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work.
  • Rafat Ali, The New Skift. The Skift founder’s argument that AI makes information cheaper and judgment more valuable, and that knowledge, a point of view, and access never get cheaper.

The future is a design problem

  • Vibhas Ratanjee and Gallup, Your Most AI-Fluent Employees Are the Most Afraid. On how believing your job will be eliminated measurably drops engagement and raises burnout, often before the technology does anything.
  • David Autor, on treating the AI future as a design problem rather than a prediction exercise, and the enormous say we have in how it actually goes.
  • Carolyn Dewar, AI Won’t Decide the Future. Leaders Will (McKinsey, via Fortune). On judgment as the thing that can’t be outsourced, and leadership as the work of staying clear-eyed under uncertainty.

title: AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about?
text:
AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about?

As more product work is generated from shared patterns, designers need to decide where an experience should surprise, celebrate, or simply leave someone alone.

Imagine asking an AI tool to design a task-completion state.

The result has a checkmark, a friendly message, and a small burst of confetti. It uses the right components. The spacing matches the system. The animation is polished.

Now imagine that same response after two different tasks.

In one, someone has finished setting up a business they have spent months trying to launch. In the other, an administrator has updated the forty-seventh record of the morning.

The component is consistent. The experiences should probably be different.

Nothing in the confetti explains which moment deserves it. That decision depends on what the person has done, how often they do it, and whether they want the product to make an occasion of it.

As AI becomes more capable of assembling interfaces from established patterns, this distinction deserves more attention. We are getting better at telling tools what belongs to our product. We also need to decide what belongs to the moment.

Matching the system is an incomplete definition of quality

There are good reasons to care about consistency. People should not have to relearn familiar actions on every screen. Teams should not spend their time reconstructing decisions already made elsewhere.

Figma’s guidance on working with its agent describes how components, guidelines, examples, and task-specific context help generated work reflect a team’s product. That is useful progress. It also makes clear that consistency depends on the context supplied to the tool.

But a faithful rendering of a system can still be an emotionally inappropriate response.

A success message can be correct and patronizing. An illustration can match the brand and occupy space someone needs for their work. A playful loading state can be charming until it appears during a time-sensitive task.

These failures are difficult to identify by inspecting the component alone. They emerge from the relationship between the component and the person encountering it.

In my earlier article about design-system judgment, I explored the distinction between enforcing rules and deciding whether a pattern is appropriate. Expression brings another version of that problem into view: a detail can follow every rule we wrote and still misunderstand the occasion.

I want software to have room for color, humor, beauty, and small surprises.

I want an interaction to feel satisfying, even when satisfaction cannot be reduced to a shorter completion time.

I also want the product to recognize when I have work to do.

Pleasure has a history beyond the AI conversation

Designers were studying this long before generative interfaces.

Don Norman’s work on emotional design considers appearance, the experience of using something, and the meaning people attach to it. That gives us a broader vocabulary than “add delight.” Pleasure can come from how something looks, how well it responds, or what owning and using it means to someone.

Therese Fessenden’s distinction between surface and deep delight is useful here too. An amusing detail can create a moment of pleasure, while a well-considered workflow can produce a quieter satisfaction that lasts through the task.

The second does not make the first disposable.

A product can be dependable and exuberant. A useful tool can have a peculiar illustration or a lovely transition simply because someone cared about making it enjoyable. We do not have to defend every expressive choice by pretending it saves three seconds.

But we do have to understand what it asks of the person.

A color choice might make a screen more inviting without adding a step. A celebration might demand attention. A joke might require cultural familiarity. A transition might make a relationship easier to understand — or force someone to wait.

“Delight” is too generous a label to apply before finding out which of those things happened.

A playful product still needs restraint

Duolingo offers an instructive example because expression is already central to its identity.

In its account of redesigning the app’s core tabs, the team describes experimenting with several visual directions, then finding tensions between consistency and purpose. An illustrated header on every tab created uniformity, but some illustrations occupied space without communicating anything useful.

The solution included different header sizes for different purposes, with titles kept in consistent positions.

That is a more useful lesson than “make every screen playful.” A recognizable product can vary its emphasis while preserving familiar structure. The team’s own account shows that even an expressive brand needs to ask where an illustration earns its space.

This matters when a design becomes an example for AI to reuse.

If the reference screen has a large illustration, should the next screen have one too? Is the illustration a general rule, a possibility, or a response to a particular situation?

A tool can reproduce the visible answer while missing the reason for it. So can a designer working from an incomplete specification.

As generation becomes easier, that missing explanation can travel further. A choice made for one meaningful moment becomes the default for several ordinary ones.

The expressive detail survives. Its purpose does not.

Consistency can include a change in tone

Mailchimp’s voice-and-tone guidance makes an important distinction: its voice remains recognizable, while its tone responds to the reader’s circumstances.

The guide welcomes humor but gives clarity priority. It asks writers to consider whether someone has finished a campaign or is confused and looking for help, and warns against forcing a joke.

This is a practical way to preserve personality without requiring the same emotional performance everywhere.

A product’s identity can live in how sensitively it changes.

Warmth during onboarding might mean encouragement. Warmth after an error might mean a direct explanation, preserved work, and a clear next step. The writing can sound like the same company without treating both situations as opportunities for comedy.

That distinction should also shape instructions given to AI.

“Make it friendly and playful” leaves a great deal unresolved. Friendly to whom? Playful at what point? What has just happened?

A more useful instruction describes the situation: the user’s work is safe; they need to understand why the action failed; avoid humor; make the recovery path obvious.

There is still room for good writing within those constraints. The constraints establish what the writing owes the person.

Expression can make an interface clearer

It is tempting to organize this debate as a negotiation between expressive design and usable design. Google’s research on Material 3 Expressive complicates that framing.

In its published research account, Google describes an email interface where the Send button became larger, more prominent, and closer to the keyboard. Participants located it faster. The expressive treatment also changed hierarchy and placement; its benefit cannot be attributed to decoration alone.

The same report includes a less successful experiment: a playlist replaced familiar rows with a scattered arrangement of album artwork. Participants found it visually exciting, but usability suffered.

These are findings from Google’s tested designs, not evidence that every product should adopt the same aesthetic. Together, they show why the actual interaction matters more than the adjective attached to it.

Color can establish emphasis. Shape can distinguish actions. Motion can show where something went. An expressive decision may help people understand a product while making it more pleasurable.

The question is what remains legible after we introduce it.

A familiar control can carry considerable character. A surprising arrangement can remove the very cues someone needs to use it. Designers have to examine both effects, rather than accepting “on brand” or “more delightful” as sufficient explanations.

The same delight can become someone else’s interruption

Asana’s celebrations show why preference belongs in this discussion.

Its 2016 introduction of an expanded celebration system described occasional animated characters appearing after task completion, with celebrations enabled through settings.

A 2018 community discussion captures the other side: a customer found the characters intrusive and asked how to disable them. A reply explained the setting.

That exchange does not establish how most users felt. It does show that the same detail can be welcome to one person and unwelcome to another.

This is where the word “delight” can hide an assumption. We describe our intention as though it were already the user’s response.

A celebration designed to recognize accomplishment may become an obstacle during repetitive work. Something enjoyed privately may feel inappropriate during a presentation. Someone may like the character and still prefer to finish without watching it.

Giving people control is part of designing the experience well.

For motion, the stakes can extend beyond preference. W3C’s guidance for Animation from Interactions, a Level AAA criterion, explains why people need ways to disable nonessential interaction-triggered movement, including the potential for vestibular symptoms.

An expressive experience should have a considered reduced-motion version. Removing movement should leave clear feedback, meaningful hierarchy, and an understandable result.

There are many ways to make something feel good. Movement is one of them.

AI changes how easily the wrong detail can spread

None of these problems began with AI. Teams have copied patterns without understanding them for years.

What AI introduces is another way to reproduce those decisions — and an opportunity to be more explicit about them.

A library might describe a celebration’s colors, duration, and animation curve. That describes the asset. It says little about whether a celebration should happen after someone completes a tutorial, pays a bill, or removes an account.

Those are different events even if the system labels all three “success.”

Here is a hypothetical rule worth testing: a fuller acknowledgment for a meaningful first achievement; brief feedback for repeated routine actions; direct, restrained language for sensitive outcomes.

That rule will not fit every product. Its value is that it gives the team something concrete to question.

Is the first achievement actually meaningful to the person, or merely valuable to our onboarding metrics? Does a repeated action become meaningful when it completes a larger goal? Are we assuming we know how someone feels because we know which button they pressed?

A good specification should leave those questions visible.

AI can help explore expressive alternatives: different copy, motion treatments, layouts, and levels of emphasis. There is no need to claim that surprise or beauty belongs exclusively to human production.

But producing an alternative and establishing when it is welcome are different kinds of work.

If we evaluate generated interfaces mainly by how closely they match the library, we will favor what is easiest to compare. If we ask whether the experience suits the occasion, we need examples, use over time, and feedback from the people living with it.

That is a broader evaluation than a screenshot review can provide.

“Worth caring about” should not mean harder to leave

There is another complication: products can use expression to serve goals people did not choose.

A cheerful character might encourage a useful habit. It might also make declining an offer feel like disappointing someone. A reward animation might acknowledge progress, or distract from how little progress actually occurred.

Those possibilities need to remain in the argument. Emotional design is capable of persuasion as well as pleasure.

The appropriate question is whose purpose the detail advances.

Does it help someone enjoy an activity they value? Does it acknowledge something they accomplished? Or does it make the product’s preferred behavior harder to refuse?

Time spent and repeat visits cannot answer that on their own. Someone may return because the product is useful, because leaving is costly, or because a mechanic creates pressure. Those explanations have different implications for design.

I am interested in software people appreciate using. That requires taking their ability to dislike a detail seriously, even when it is the detail the team loves most.

Give the expressive decision a proper review

In a product team, this work needs a place before the final polish pass.

For a proposed expressive moment, I would want to see it in three conditions: the first encounter, repeated use, and a situation where the person is rushed or something has gone wrong.

The same animation may behave beautifully in isolation and become tiring in a sequence. The same line of copy may be reassuring on a quiet afternoon and dismissive during a failure.

Research should make room for those differences. Watch whether people can continue. Ask what they think the response means. Find out whether they want to see it again. Include people who prefer less motion or sound, and test whether the experience still communicates clearly.

These observations will not produce a universal delight score. They can help us distinguish a detail people value from one they tolerate.

This also changes what we document.

Alongside the approved example, record the circumstance it serves, when to scale it back, and a case where it should not be used. Give both people and AI tools a reason to choose differently.

A system with that kind of guidance can protect character. It can make room for an unusual illustration, a distinctive rhythm, or a moment of celebration while keeping everyday work dependable.

The alternative is to encode only what is easy to repeat and hope the rest survives delivery.

I want the products we build with AI to have more room for pleasure: a color choice that lifts a screen, a response that acknowledges effort, a transition that feels unusually right. I also want that pleasure to survive actual use, beyond the first demo and the designer’s own preferences.

Return to the two completed tasks. The new business owner and the administrator may both need confirmation. One might welcome a moment to take in what they have accomplished. The other might want the next record ready.

AI can generate both responses.

We still have to notice that the occasions are different.

title: What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us
text:
What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us

Three design experts told me how AI is changing the way we build and maintain Design Systems. And led me to think that “the future” is already happening now.

You’ve probably read, or even written, one of those LinkedIn posts about someone building a complete Design System in 20 minutes with Claude. Or in 15 minutes with Gemini. Or… you get the idea.

Those posts made me curious. I had never built a full Design System, although I had set up the basic elements of one before I really dug into AI, and it was as interesting as it was painful. So the promise of building a full one in minutes was appealing.

My mistake? Confusing a UI kit with a Design System, and believing the whole process could really be done in minutes.

At UXDX Berlin last May, two talks about Design Systems made me want to know more about how AI has changed them in the day-to-day of product teams. That curiosity led me to interview three design experts, and to get to the essential part of what a Design System actually is: Marianne Ashton-Booth, Head of Product Design at ITV; David Sward, Chief Design Officer at Siemens; and Nicolas Chatelain, freelance Senior Designer and specialized in Design System and Ops.

Three experts, three different approaches. Nicolas Chatelain bets on a frame that bends without breaking, flexible with teams and ready for AI. David Sward bets on speed with guardrails, with AI as a tool and a human in the loop. Marianne Ashton-Booth bets on people and process, treating the Design System like a product.

The last two had both just given a talk at UXDX when I talked with them, so what follows draws on two different moments with each of them: what they said on stage, and what they told me one-on-one afterwards.

1. AI automates the easy part, but the hard part still belongs to humans

One-on-one after her talk, Marianne Ashton-Booth said something that felt particularly on point to me: “Anybody can spin up prototypes in minutes, and that’s great. But then that gap between what’s actually feasible, what’s actually close to the brand, or close to the actual components that we’ve got, can be quite distant.”

Nicolas Chatelain, whom I interviewed in July, put the same idea in other words: the UI is the easy part of a Design System. “The hardest part, the one that makes a DS work or not, is governance and adoption.”

Neither of them sees the components as the problem; Nicolas even says anyone could, indeed, build a kit while we were talking. What matters is consistency across teams, and across a whole company, and that is the human part of a Design System. A Zeroheight report on the state of Design Systems, published in early 2026, points the same way: 59% of practitioners credit communication and community for their system’s adoption.

On stage, Marianne Ashton-Booth had already named what breaks instead. When a design system fails, she said, “it’s almost never just [the design system’s core operations]. The components are usually fine.” What breaks are the invisible layers underneath: trust, communication, prioritisation, relationships, and shared belief.

2. The bottleneck has moved from production speed to review

“My biggest problem is trying to slow people down with AI,” David Sward told me. Indeed, AI has sped up a lot of processes, all the way to delivery.

Here, he does not mean slowing his team down so that they get used to AI, but keeping them inside the security and compliance rules of a large enterprise. With hundreds of products relying on his system, a mistake would take several hundred million euros to fix. His operating principle: “don’t break things.”

But the fact remains: productivity has risen. And once speed is there, the bottleneck shifts from production to the people who review, validate and keep everything coherent. Nicolas Chatelain and Marianne Ashton-Booth ran into this too.

During Nicolas Chatelain’s mission for an international group, for example, AI-boosted product teams started to outpace the central Design System team, whose original strategy was to lock everything down. His verdict:

“With AI, it’s a total rollback. We have to become much more flexible, because tomorrow people could create a kit in five minutes. If we become useless, they’ll find an even easier way to bypass us.”

Figma’s slots, which let teams put their own content inside a standardised component, are one way to loosen the frame.

At ITV, Marianne Ashton-Booth’s team takes another route and relies on “design system reps” in both design and engineering: “They tend to be the go-to people that have a little bit more prominence and involvement in things like final decisions. It just means that things can keep moving rather than just becoming a bit of a bottleneck.” On stage, she added that rather than treating AI as a separate topic, ITV asked the right question: “What does that mean for the design system? How should our processes evolve?”

These three approaches suggest that there is no single way to handle the bottleneck: it depends on the context, the level of risk, and how far AI has advanced, and been accepted, in the organisation. That is precisely where humans remain useful: understanding at what moment, and to what extent, everyone who holds decision-making power over the Design System should step in, and when they should let go.

3. The Design System is becoming something AI reads

This is the part that sounds most like “the future”, but is actually already the present: making the system readable for machines.

Nicolas Chatelain’s team started watching tools like V0 and Lovable in the second half of 2025, and concluded it was too early to adopt them. They chose to prepare the system instead: tokens migrated to the DTCG (Design Tokens Community Group) standard, a shared format for the values of a system, like colours, spacing or typography, so that every tool, and every AI agent, reads them the same way.

An MCP server (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI agent query the Design System directly, for instance to find the right component or token, instead of guessing. In a field study published in July 2026, Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent looked at 21 open-source Design Systems: 20 of them offer an MCP server (official or community-built), but only 3 have set up Figma Code Connect, which ties a Figma component to its real code counterpart. Plenty of systems let AI read them, far fewer tie their components back to design.

David Sward’s team uses AI on the other side of the process: a large language model (LLM) compares what teams have implemented with what the Design System is supposed to be, and, in his words, “systematically tells you what to fix.” In his own Design System, AI stays “a tool just like anything else” (an engine harmonises thousands of icons, for instance), and his broader principle holds: “You can’t remove a human from the loop and then expect them to step back in to operate the system if they don’t understand the state the system is in.”

Marianne Ashton-Booth, on her end, is adamant: “There might be parts of [a design system] that become more AI-generated or automated. But a design system isn’t just that part, you know, it’s the people and it’s the process as well. And that’s the bit that I think we’ll still retain.”

Where I think we’re heading: code as the source of truth

These insights led me to believe this is where Design Systems are heading: the code, rather than the design file, is becoming their source of truth. We might already be there. Designers who use AI seem to open Figma less and less (that’s my case), and in teams where shipping and iterating beat perfecting details, the blurring of roles (I talked about it here) doesn’t help.

Nicolas Chatelain said it: “Today, the source of truth has to be the code. Absolutely.” Working in the code removes a layer of abstraction between AI and production, and “tomorrow, when this documentation lives directly in the code, we won’t need Figma anymore.” He admits he may be “completely wrong”, and still finds Figma useful to explore and fine-tune. And I agree with him that Figma isn’t dead. But for me its place in the process has definitely changed.

Concretely, it means that whatever is merged into the code becomes the standard, and design files, documentation and AI agents all read from it. Every review then becomes a governance decision. But as Tony Ward wrote in his recent article “Code as the Source of Truth”, the key is to keep “a subject-matter expert in the loop at every step of the way.” Which leaves the real question: in this new process, who gets to say what goes into the truth?

As for me, meeting these three experts showed me there is no single answer to that question. Each built theirs from their own environment, and in that richness I found keys to meet my own challenges. I hope you will too.

Thanks to UXDX for providing access to the event, and to David Sward, Marianne Ashton-Booth and Nicolas Chatelain for their time.

All of Nicolas Chatelain’s quotes were translated from French.
